utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On this Monday, I'd like to say good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused. I can see that some of the Defence don't all seem to be there but the accused are. We are going to continue the proceedings with a witness in a moment, but before we have the witness shown in, I have three oral decisions, three oral rulings, and I would also like to go into private session for another matter. First oral decision with respect to the admission of exhibits relevant to Witness CE. With respect to witness CE who appeared on the 23rd of November, 2006, and the exhibits that were presented to the witness, the Chamber has decided to admit the following exhibits presented by the Prosecution, and we're doing so because they have a certain amount of probative value and relevance. I'm going to read them out slowly to avoid any mistakes: P 09750 under seal; P 00462 under seal; P 02215, P 02607; P 03075; P 03160; P 03222; P 03347; P 07529; P 07533; P 09745 under seal; and P 09746. The Chamber would like to note that P 02319 [as interpreted] has already been admitted through CD, Witness CD. P 03019. P 03019 is the number. I see there was a mistake. The Chamber has decided to admit the following evidence presented by the Defence of Mr. Stojic because they consider that it has certain probative value and relevance: 2D 00272. The Chamber has decided to admit the following exhibits presented by the Defence of Mr. Petkovic with the motivation that they have certain probative value and relevance: P 06916. Exhibit 4D 00408 is admitted and as identification until the document has been translated. So it will be marked for identification. The Chamber has also decided to admit the following four documents which have been marked for identification and once they are translated into English because they have certain probative value and relevance: 4D 00033; 4D 00034; 4D 00035; and 4D 00036. Second oral decision, second oral ruling: The Chamber will state its views with respect to documents related to Witness CF and the Chamber has decided to admit the following exhibits presented by the Prosecution because they represent a certain degree of credibility, probative value, and relevance, and I'm going to read out slowly: P 09751 under seal; P 09752 under seal; paragraph 55 of Exhibit P 06697. There's a mistake; it is P 06697. P 08192 [as interpreted]. Another mistake. P 08792. P 09557; P 09558. The Chamber has decided not to admit P 09764 because the Witness CF did not recognise the locality shown on the photograph. The Chamber takes note that the exhibits P 02215, P 02215, P 03160, P 08742, and P 09038 presented by the Prosecution have already been admitted. The Chamber would also like to note that the Defence counsel did not ask for the tendering of any documents during testimony of Witness CF. And now the last oral ruling having to do with Witness Hasan Hasic. The witness appeared on the 27th of November, 2006. The Chamber decides to admit the following exhibits presented by the Prosecution because it considers that they have certain probative value and relevance: There are four numbers that I'm going to read out P 04822, P 09747, P 09748, and IC 00116. The Chamber takes note that the Defence did not ask for the tendering of any exhibits. With respect to exhibits that are waiting, now, with respect to Witness CB, I should like to ask the Prosecution to specify or, rather, the legal assistant, the pages of P 04698 that it wishes to tender into evidence. I should also like to invite the parties to furnish IC lists for Witness CL. As far as Witness Salko Bojcic is concerned for which we have already received the lists for 2D. We should also like to request IC lists for Witness CN and also the IC list for CO. With respect to that particular witness, we have the Prosecution list for Witness CO. We should also like to request the -- a list from the Defence for Witness CP. We also have the Prosecution list for that same witness. We hope that those lists will come in before the end of the week. I'm going to ask the registrar to give me the IC numbers, because we have four lists.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] List of documents tendered through 2D through Witness CM will be given Exhibit them IC 163. List of documents of 2D through Witness Salko Bojcic will be given Exhibit number IC 164. The Prosecution exhibits tendered through Witness CO will be given Exhibit number IC 165. And Prosecution Exhibits tendered through Witness CP will be given Exhibit number IC 166. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going to ask the registrar to go into private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, between the period late 1992 leading into 1993, what kind of a relationship existed as between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims in Stolac and its surrounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not bad until just before the rounding up into camps, and then tensions began just before people were rounded up. It was obvious that something was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: When you say it was obvious, could you give us some kind of indication as to how it was so obvious? What signs did you notice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we noticed that Croats and Muslims did not mingle any more, did not socialise any more, did not sit together in cafes and bars, and that's how we felt that there was something going on, that somebody prohibited these two groups from socialising.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And are you in a position to say what actually motivated this change in relationship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably it was the HDZ party, because they led all this. They managed all this. They advised people what to do. They told them what to do. I don't know what they were seeking.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, now you talk about a deterioration in relationship. Was there a particular time when this culminated finally, when the parties were no longer friends, that they broke apart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 3rd of July. Until the 3rd of July on the combat lines everybody was together, Muslims and Croats, and what happened on the 3rd of July was simply horrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: What year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Where were you exactly on the 3rd of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 3rd of July, I was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Rotimlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Had you visited Stolac at all on the 3rd of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 3rd of July -- I did go to Stolac on the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well you talk about the 3rd of July being the -- the date on which the relationships severely deteriorated. Can you tell us how or what -- what happened if you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On the 3rd of July, I saw when the rounding up started in the settlement, when HVO soldiers arrived in large numbers and started going from house to house rounding up all the able-bodied men of military ages and even some older than military age.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: This was in the village of Rotimlja, I think you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Where did this take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That happened where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And that was close by Stolac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And where did you -- where were you when you observed this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 3rd of July, I was at Rotimlja. On the 3rd of July, I was at Rotimlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But I'm asking you about -- when you observed these people being rounded up that you described, you said it was where you lived.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Was this in Rotimlja or was it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's in Borojevici.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Where exactly were you in Borojevici when you saw this happen, were you on the street or in your car or so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me try to explain. I noticed, in fact a lot of us noticed a large number of troops that had arrived, and we fled. Whoever could flee, fled. I don't know. Nobody was expecting that this would happen, that people would be rounded up. Some people still trusted that nothing bad would happen. They stayed behind, and some others fled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not very clear, Witness. I have the impression that you are avoiding answers. The Prosecutor asked you where you were. We have finally understood that you were in the village of Borojevici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were in that village. Can you tell us what happened in that village? Did HVO arrive and entered the first houses, arrested the people there those houses, after which you decided to run away? Briefly explain to us what you saw with your own eyes and what you did yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw people being taken away, that is, I saw my brother and my neighbour being taken away. Then I went into hiding and saved myself from being rounded up on that day at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who arrested your brother and your neighbour, who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this HVO military police, from which battalion were they, from which unit? Do you know the unit of that military police? Because military police is a very large notion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military police from Stolac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. And why did you flee yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I didn't trust them. I knew something bad would happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time you were a member of the ABiH. Were you wearing the uniform of the ABiH on that day or were you in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were on leave? How come that you were not in your brigade? You were on leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was on leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Flynn, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So on observing these arrests and decide to go flee, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went back towards Rotimlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what did you find and who did you meet in Rotimlja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came across some of the people from Stolac, and they told me what was going on and that this rounding up was being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did they tell you where the rounding up was being carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were rounding people up, first of all in the towns and convince and then along the front lines, the combat lines. All the soldiers who were up at the lines were rounded up and all people brought from other municipalities and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did they tell you which units had been target for these arrests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which units were being arrested. Well, it was all the military police, and there were people who were brought in from Mostar, Ljubuski, and Citluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Rotimlja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what did you do during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did what was necessary. I did the work that I was ordered to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you observe any further arrests during those three days that you were in Rotimlja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, at the time you were a military man, a member of the Bregava Brigade, and you were an eyewitness of the arrests undertaken by the HVO. Why did you not go back to your unit straight away? Perhaps you tried. Did you tell your unit that there were problems? Did you warn them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, I didn't. I didn't inform them. There was somebody else, I suppose, who was supposed to do that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if everybody did what you did and thought that it was up to someone else, then the authority of the Bregava Brigade -- the authorities of the Bregava Brigade might not have known what was going on, on the ground, if nobody informed them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm sure they did know. Everybody had their assignment, so I couldn't meddle in things like that. I wouldn't know who to report to or inform, but I knew what my job was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was a driver on standby, whenever needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the role of a driver, you would have to be next to your truck; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we took turns. There were shifts. There were several trucks and several drivers, so we would take it in turns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: From what you saw and from what you heard, can you tell us what happened to those people that were arrested within the HVO and other people who were arrested? Do you know what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were loaded up onto trucks and driven off to camps, Gabela and Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I want to -- you have a booklet of documents in front of you. If you look to your right. And I want you to turn to exhibit number -- the tab is 3222. You have a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, the interpreters would like to ask you to speak up and approach the microphone so that they can hear you better.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You have a document dated the 6th of July, 1993, which is issued by the commander of the HVO, Colonel Obradovic, and in paragraph 1 -- it's an order, and in paragraph 1 he orders that all remaining Muslims in the units of the HVO be removed from the existing records, disarmed, and imprisoned. And this is addressed to other HVO units. Is this what happened on the ground as you remember it and as what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after the 6th of July, 1993, what did you decide to do? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where did I go. Well, I don't know. I went back to Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Where did you go in Stolac, and who did you meet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met with a group of those people, and they told me what was going on and what happened in Stolac, that they were rounding people up and taking them to camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you make any decisions as to what you would do yourself then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well -- well, I don't know. I decided something. I went back to Rotimlja, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: After the 6th of July did you meet your family again in Borojevici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did meet my father and my grandmother and all the other elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you make a decision what to do considering that there had been arrests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We decided to escape to the woods and hide there because we thought it would all be over quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did your mother go with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, she wasn't with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How about your grandmother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My granny was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And where did your mother go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mother went to -- well, she was rounded up with the other younger women. They were all rounded up, and then they were taken to -- well, it was like a camp. It was at the school in Aladinici. All the women were taken there, and the elderly people who could walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And who rounded them up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The same military police which had carried out the arrests earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, arrests.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And after Aladinici do you know where your mother went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were at Aladinici and transferred to Buna, and from Buna to Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And was this a voluntary transfer? Did they go willingly? Did they volunteer to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not voluntary, no. They were forced, forcibly displaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, those soldiers. Somebody ordered them. The party, who else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And how long did your mother spend in Aladinici, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't really know. Eight or nine days, I think. They were there in very difficult circumstances: No water, no food, one on top of another, a small space.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is this something you were told or you know for a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see it personally. My mother told me about it and all the other women that spent time in that school. The Stolac plateau is a large area. There were a lot of women and young girls and children there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move back to your group. Your group, how many were in them -- in your group all together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sixteen, 16 of us in the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were these men and women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just men.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And where -- where exactly doing go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where did we go? We went to hide in the hope that everything would be over soon, that we wouldn't have to be in hiding for long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Witness. We have to be more precise, because the Judges are extremely precise. You explained to us that on the 3rd of July you were on leave from the ABiH and that you were a member of the Bregava Brigade and that you had escaped, and we discovered that you were in hiding for a few weeks. And you've just told us that there were 16 of you. So you were hiding. Where were you hiding? What were you doing with the other members of the group? Did you put up any resistance? Were you armed at all? Did you think that your military unit might have thought that you had deserted if it didn't receive any word from you? So quite simply, in a word, what were you doing amongst that group? You were spending the days hiding in a hole, or did you undertake any military action? Could you be more specific about all those points, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we were hiding in the hope, and I'm repeating this, that everything would end quickly. We were hiding in the woods, in the forest. As luck would have it, the weather was rather good. There were some tents. Some people had some at the present time, but as I say, we all hoped it would all be over soon and we could go back home. We did not put any resistance. We were unarmed. We were all wearing civilian clothes at the time. I was on leave at home. Nobody had any arms or uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How did you manage for provisions while you were hiding in the woods? Food.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last house in that particular area, well, we would stand on guard. Two men would do what was necessary, and we got our food that way to survive. At one end of the village, in my uncle house there was the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And how long did you manage to stay hidden, your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our group was in hiding until the 25th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us what happened on the 25th of September, 1993? Who came, what happened, where you were taken, and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 25th of September we were surrounded in the woods. We were surrounded by the Croatian soldiers, the HVO police, and were taken -- we had to walk to -- well, three and a half kilometres to a vehicle that was waiting for us, and then they transported us to the Kostana hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And how -- how were you treated when they originally found and arrested you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were rough with us. They beat us. They abused us, insulted us, swore at as us. They used bad language. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And among this group who you were with, was there elderly people and young people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Witness, if you had to name names -- or if you're going to name names, we'll have to do it in private session. So take care, Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I was going to do that. I was going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: As I asked you, among your group did you have underage persons and elderly persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some underage persons and two elderly persons. Not too old but elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Perhaps now would be an appropriate time to ask to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's move into private session for a few moments and then we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you was -- was whether you were conscious when you arrive at Gabela. Do you remember arriving to Gabela?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In I may just interrupt. Excuse me, sir. Is the Prosecutor suggesting that he was unconscious? You know, in other words that he had been unconscious and transported over there, or is he asking him whether he recalls going there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Simply I'm asking -- I'll rephrase it and I'll say --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: -- do you remember arriving at Gabela?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember because that day -- or, rather, in Kostana hospital I received so many blows that I was left completely immobile, and I passed out. I was unconscious. I didn't know what was going on. I was totally unconscious and wasn't able to move. So that's why I don't remember when I arrived or how I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in this state of unconsciousness following -- on arrival at Gabela?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Upon arrival -- or, rather, after my arrival, 37 or 8 days I was immobile throughout at that time and I was unconscious. I might have said something, but I wasn't able to speak coherently. I was sort of deranged mostly, couldn't put two and two together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said that you arrived in Gabela when you were unconscious, and that apparently according to what you told us you were in that state for 37 days not knowing exactly what you said or what you were doing. So in other words you were in a coma, that would mean you were in a coma, and there were stages to a coma, stage 1, 2, 3, but you can't be left for 37 days without eating anything, without drinking anything on pain of death. Do you remember eating at all, or was it a period that, as far as you're concerned, is something you absolutely don't remember now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not 37 but 27 or 28 days. I don't know what period of time. It was a long period of time. And we didn't receive any food for a long period of time. How can I explain that to you? You didn't see the state I was in. I was in such a terrible state, just skin and bones. We did get something, but that was just by chance, now and again. They would throw in -- there was this iron door to this hangar, no windows or anything, and some food would be thrown in, and if you managed to get a piece of something, you did. If you didn't, you would just die. And the same applied to water. But we didn't receive water or food for long periods of time. And as I said, and begging your pardon, people would urinate and then drink that urine once it was cold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During that period did a doctor come to see you at Gabela to diagnose you, to bring you some medicines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not once. Never ever did a doctor come or bring so much as a pill. There was a man from Stolac, last name Ljiljak, I can't remember his first name, but he had a pill or two to give me two or three times, because I had fractured ribs which made all movement very painful. I think it was three or four times that he gave me some pills. And he gave me -- he gave some pills to my father.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Looking at you, you seem to be a strong man. You look quite strong. But when you left Gabela, how many kilos had you lost, how much weight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, honestly I don't know how much weight I lost, but I looked horrible. You see how tall I am and I was skin and bone. I looked skeletal. And of course what can you expect when there was no regular food, no regular drink. It was inhuman. Other people can confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among the questions -- after the questions of the Presiding Judge, I would like to ask one. Were you aware of any visits of international organisations such as the ICRC? Did anybody come to Gabela?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Once or twice, I think, we were visited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when they came, was it during that period when you got almost nothing to eat and when people had to go to the bathroom in the conditions that you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When people from the ICRC came to see you, did they examine your skin, your appearance, your ribs? Did they realise the condition you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They came to the entrance to the hangar, but nobody came in. Nobody walked around, not from the ICRC. Nobody looked at me. Nobody examined me for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they saw you from afar, from the entrance to the hangar. Nobody came in, nobody came close to you, nobody talked with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nobody came in. Nor did they come close or ask us questions. There were many people in the same state as myself. They distributed some sort of packages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After this visit of the ICRC, did you feel a significant change in the living conditions at Gabela, or did it continue just the same as before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything was exactly the same as before. But just before we left for Heliodrom, a few days before we left things changed a little. They would let us, for instance, outside to take a walk outside the hangar and go as far as the entrance to the camp. So we could talk between the gate and the hangar. As for the rest, there was no improvement, and the hygiene did not improve either. Even then, there was just a pail for going to the bathroom for 400 people or -- I don't know exactly we were, but they all watched my father help me onto the pail, and it was a total disaster, a total disgrace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because you cool not go to the pail being in the condition in which you were, and you had to be helped onto the pail to relieve yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, because my balance was also disrupted. Something was damaged in my brain, and whenever I would try to walk straight I would start leaning to the right. And I -- unless stopped, I would simply fall to the ground. That's why I had to be helped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later, when you were liberated, when there was peace again, did you go to see doctors? Did you have a CAT scan of your head to see if there was internal damage? Did you have any medical examination of your head to establish if there were any permanent consequences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did all that. And all that medical file has been turned over to OTP investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you gave your entire medical file to investigators.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the Prosecution is not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: We are aware of a number of medical reports, Your Honours. There was a question of some photographs of injuries sustained, but unfortunately these weren't passed on to us, but a copy of the medical report was. It's very brief, and I will be putting it to the witness, but the documents provided by the Bosnian authorities were quite small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would you explain, Mr. Flynn, what you mean by saying "they were not passed to us."

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The Bosnian authorities presented to us related to this period of time, they gathered certain information from various witnesses who had been held in Gabela and various other camps, and they compiled large dossiers, and the investigators with interviews with the Bosnian authorities were presented with these dossiers. But the dossiers would not have been as complete as we would have liked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: What makes you affirm here that there were actually documents, photographs in existence that were not put at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, in the statements which the -- the witness has given, he makes mention to -- about photographs which he says, "You have," and he's addressing the Bosnian authorities. But we don't have that photographs. So that's my only conclusion, that there were photographs handed over to the Bosnian authorities, but unfortunately they did not find their way here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when you met with the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, did you give the investigators your medical file?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All that I had I gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To whom? To the authorities of your country or to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The investigator of the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what I'm telling Your Honours is when the investigators took the statement from this witness, they did have a number of documents which had earlier been presented to them by the Bosnian authorities. The AID statement that was made in 1996. They were also presented with a video statement made by this witness, and presented with a doctor's report. But there's no indication from the documents which we were furnished that any photographs whatsoever were furnished to us, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you have any occasion to visit any of the other accommodations in Gabela?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had one occasion before I was moved to Heliodrom to go into hangar number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So do I understand it that the only two hangars you saw were your own hanger and hangar number 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were four hangars in Gabela in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: No, but what I'm asking you is, how many of those hangars did you visit and see the conditions of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was in one hangar, and I saw the conditions in one more hangar, number 3, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Was number 3 any better than the conditions in your hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was exactly the same. What could possibly be better? Everything is the same. All those hangars were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Tell us, can you -- do you know who was in charge of the camp at the time you were held there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean who was in charge of the whole camp. Bosko Previsic was the main man, and his deputy was Nikola Andrun.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could you tell us how Mr. Previsic treated the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how he -- what to tell you. He was capable of killing people. I heard that from two men. It's no -- no way for a reasonable man to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you know anybody personally that he is alleged to have killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Please tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted). He was killed by this Bosko Previsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you know the circumstances under which he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are in open session and he just gave the name of his cousin. Can we please have an appropriate order for redaction prepared. Mr. Flynn, you should have thought about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. The fact that this gentleman had passed away ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hope I'm not wrong, but I don't think this killing is in the indictment. As -- if it goes to relevance, maybe we could refer to what is in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is relevant is to know the conduct of the person who was in charge on that establishment. Registrar, would you please prepare the order. Mr. Flynn, we are going to be forced -- we are going to be forced to take a 30-minute break. How much time do you need to conclude --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Not very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Because we have to deal with Heliodrom yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Not very long, Your Honour. I believe that I have approximately 10 more questions, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are taking the break now, and resuming at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just a point of information for Your Honours on what Mr. Kovacic mentioned. Over the break, we just checked on it, and it appears that the killing of Mustafa Obradovic is part of the indictment, and it is specifically mentioned in the confidential annex paragraph 200. I thought you'd might like to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Before we broke, Witness, you were telling us about this incident with Mustafa Obradovic and how he had been killed. Very briefly, can you tell us what happened from what you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mustafa Obradovic, with quite a number of others, other inmates, he was doing forced labour at the Grabovina barracks or thereabouts. Now, at the end of this bout of labour, he happened to come by a loaf of bread or whatever. And when they returned to camp, Boko Previsic lined them up when they got off the truck and ordered them to take out any food they had, which they did, but he tried to hide this piece of bread. But the man came by and found the piece of bread and what happened, happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you personally have any contact with this Mr. Previsic or any other senior official in Gabela?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, never any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you have contact with any other official in Gabela?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no contacts. Just that day when we arrived, and the six or seven days that we were in those premises with the man, Marinko Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Who was this man Marinko Markovic, and what happened with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marinko Maric. He was in the SIS. It was the Croatian -- well, some sort of secret service or whatever. All I know is that it was called SIS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Flynn. I would like to come back to the episode with Mustafa Obradovic. Witness, you have said what happened, happened; and that is definitely true. But it is not really precise. Could you tell us more precisely what occurred when -- when this piece of bread had been found?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. And then a follow-up question for you to be able to answer properly. You -- were you witness to this incident, or were you told about the incident by others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see it with my own eyes. My relatives who were in that line, line-up, told me, and the man who took the bread.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session so avoid mentioning names. Otherwise, we're going to have to redact them. So please don't name names. So you've just told us that they were close relatives of yours who told you about this incident; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can you be more specific about the details, because my colleague would like to know the details of the incident. Can you do that for us? Any specific features of the incident, and who killed him in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was killed by Bosko Previsic. First of all, he took out a pistol and cocked it, but probably there wasn't any ammunition. And then he shot at him. Then one of the guards took a rifle and shot at him, shot him in the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So one of the guards killed him; is that right? Not Previsic himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Previsic killed him. He took the rifle. He shot from a pistol. There was no ammunition in the pistol. Then he grabbed a rifle from a guard and then he personally shot at him and shot him in the head and he was dead on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on the basis of what they told you all this was done in the presence of the others, was it, that went out to do forced labour and had come back and witnessed the scene; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They were standing there and saw all this happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And just as a follow-up yes to what Their Honours were asking you, what was the specific reason that this man was shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The specific reason for the killing was the discovery of this piece of bread that the man had tried to hide. He put something in front of the piece of bread to hide it. But the truth of it is that he hid the piece of bread. And since the man had issued orders that everything, all food and everything should be placed in front of the men, he tried to hide it in order to eat it. Because he was angry that his orders hadn't been obeyed, he killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Just to conclude on this subject, can I show you, with the assistance of the usher, if possible, Exhibit 09271. This is a certificate of death which refers to a Mustafa, son of -- a Mustafa Obradovic, born on the 1st of the 2nd, 1974. Is this the gentleman that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a few moments ago that this occurred after he had been out to do forced labour. What can you tell us about this? Were there people taken out to do forced labour from the camp, and did this happen often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, often. It happened often. They were taken out to do forced labour often. People were taken to work on private property, private land. And in the camp compound, they were forced to work with their bare hands and pluck the weeds or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you ever actually witness yourself people taken out to do forced labour while you were held in Gabela?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I came to, when I regained consciousness, I know that they were taken out. Trucks would arrive to collect them and drive them off to do forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived to Gabela, was the group that had been held with you in Kostana, did they all come with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Suad wasn't. Suad was buried in the cemetery of Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But the remainder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The remainder, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did they all survive Gabela as you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ibro died shortly after his arrival in Gabela, Ibro Razic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know how he died or why he died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ibro died succumbing to the blows and the abuse and mistreatment at Kostana hospital in Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can I refer you to the booklet of documents which you have in front of you, and would you look at Exhibit 08302. This is a certificate of death for the person you mentioned, Ibro Razic, and it gives a date of birth. It also mentions members of his family on the second paragraph. Can you confirm to us, does this certificate refer to the same Ibro that you told us died in Gabela?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's the same Ibro.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Now, how long were you held in Gabela?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Witness, there's a certificate of the death which says that he died in Gabela. I understood it that as far as you were concerned, you thought that he died in the hospital. So where did he die, in fact, in the hospital or in Gabela?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not in the hospital. He didn't die in hospital. He died in Gabela, at the entrance to the Gabela camp where we were interrogated by --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Just so there's no misunderstanding, the witness did make reference to another gentleman dying in Kostana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you say that Ibro Razic died at the entrance to Gabela camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the room we were interrogated in, that's where he died. Upon arrival from Kostana hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So he died as a result of the bad treatment in Kostana hospital or bad treatment in Gabela camp? Which?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He died as the result of abuse in Kostana hospital and partially also in the -- from the treatment in Gabela, the blows in Kostana hospital. And the same thing happened for a short time in Gabela as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for explaining that to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, I was asking you how long -- for how long you were kept in Gabela.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in Gabela from the 2nd of October until the 15th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what happened on the 15th of December, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 15th of December, 1993, what happened was this: All the elderly people and those who weren't on the list of the army of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were exchanged in Mostar, and we who were on that army list were transferred to Heliodrom camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you remember how many ABiH people were transferred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can I just refer you to a report which is Exhibit 07184, again with the assistance of Madam Usher. If you turn to the Bosnian page, you'll see that this is a report of the Capljina military police dated the 15th of December, 1993. And if you go down, you'll see it says "Report," and it talks about the transfer of military prisoner of war from the military prison in Gabela to Heliodrom military prison. And on the -- later on the page it talks about -- and it then talks about the number 406. And there's mention of 401. So you talked about your transfer to Gabela -- from Gabela to Heliodrom on the 15th of December. Does this -- does this report reflect what happened on at that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may. With all due respect, we've gone over this -- this sort of introduction of evidence in the past. The gentleman can introduce this document by other means and then point to Your Honours to take into consideration that one reflects the other. But to ask the gentleman to verify the contents of the document, in my opinion, is not the best way to consume time, especially when the Prosecution is saying that, you know, they're pressed for time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to labour this issue, but the witness did give evidence that he was transferred from Gabela to Heliodrom on the 15th of December. This report talks about such transfers, and I want to know whether or not the report reflects actually what he remembers and what he told us about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He didn't generate the report. That's my whole point, Your Honours. Nothing prevents the Prosecution from introducing the report. The gentleman can vouch for the contents of the report. You have the testimony of the witness, live testimony, the best evidence. Then you can say, "Here's the evidence. Here's the report." If they -- if they can connect and they can marry the report with the evidence, that's sufficient. I just think that this is not the best way to -- to use our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: My only response to that again, Your Honour, and I don't want to belabour on the issue, but this is the way it's been presented over the last couple of weeks, and there are many documents which have been presented to witnesses which they cannot obviously address themselves. They have never seen before. But it has been put to them that the contents of their document reflects either what they have told or the position that they knew on the ground, and that's all we're asking. We're not asking them to verify the report. We're not asking them to authenticate the report. We're just asking them does their evidence correspond with what's written in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Very well. I have no objections to that. But I just want to be noted on the record, this is a waste of prosecutorial time. That's what I want the record to reflect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Flynn, in addressing the document, the document has to do with prisoners of war. So there's a question that you should have asked the witness, but I'm going to ask him now. Sir, when you were transferred from Gabela or, rather, from the day that you were arrested up until the day you were released, were you -- did you consider yourself to be a prisoner of war or a civilian prisoner? What would you say? In your opinion, what were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, normally -- well, I've already said. I was a member of the BH army. At the point of my arrest, I was wearing civilian clothes. I wasn't wearing a uniform. So I don't know. I don't know how to answer that question, what I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you were in civilian clothes when you were arrested, at the moment of your arrest, but officially speaking, you were a member of the BH army; right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the authorities who detained you could consider they were detaining a member from the opposite military camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this document speaks about the transfer of prisoners of war from Gabela to Heliodrom. Now, what about the figures in the document? Would you say they were correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the number was, but I was among those, yes. I was among -- I was among those transferred from Gabela to Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So all you can tell us is that you were among those transferred from Gabela to Heliodrom. Now, a follow-up question. A moment ago, you were talking about forced labour, and you quoted an example which I was rather surprised to hear, but perhaps you could explain this. You said that the prisoners were picking weeds in the prison. Now, if you were a prisoner of war, was it forbidden to pick weeds in the prison? And if you were given orders to do so, would that be forced labour? I'd like to hear your opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, forced labour. Yes, this was forced -- the labour of -- people didn't have any skin left on their hands, and it was these brambles, thorny brambles that they had to pluck, and their skin was all torn. I didn't see that, but it was terrible. I know people who lived through this. I know people personally who had to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that those people who were plucking thorny brambles damaged their hands because they didn't have any protection and their hands were in a very poor state. Is that what we're to understand? Because we've all, of course, plucked weeds, but these were thorny brambles, and I can understand what happened. And you, too, were probably asked to pull bramble in Gabela. Now, why is this different from weeding your garden, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not ordinary weeds or grass. It's called thorny bramble, and these were low-growing, young plants and there are a lot of thorns. So it's difficult to do this with your own hands. It would scathe your hands and your skin. And that's why they were told to do that. It was taking out on the prisoners, forcing them to work with these thorny brambles. It's not ordinary weeds or grass, it was thorny brambles on these seedlings, and it's terrible what these people were forced to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So you're giving us this new element now. You say that these people who were ordered to pick the thorny brambles, that this was intentional on the part of the person issuing the order because they knew that these brambles had thorns on them and that this would hurt the hands of the people who were forced to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, yes. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could you tell us, did -- did forced labour continue when you were in Heliodrom. Were people taken out of the camp for forced labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the Heliodrom as well people were taken out to do forced labour on the front lines and Ljubuski and Bijaca. They were taken to done some kind of work, but it was forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did all of these people manage to come back? Did they return to Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some were wounded and some were killed on the front lines while we were working to fortify HVO bunkers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you give us a number of those who were killed, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that quite a few people were killed, but there was one man who came from us -- from Gabela to Heliodrom. I know that one person in particular who was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give us one name of somebody who was killed on the front line who had been at Heliodrom and was taken out and didn't come back because they were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know the last name. It was Jazvin, but I really don't know his first name. I knew the man. I knew him well by sight but I can't remember his first name. The last name was Jazvin. He had come with us from Gabela and he got killed while fortifying bunkers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on the front line while fortifying bunkers he was killed. By who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know, but he definitely did not come back. He was killed. I don't know by whom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I know that he was exchanged, but I don't know who killed him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was exchanged. When you say that, you mean his body was exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, his body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How would you describe the conditions in Heliodrom compared to Gabela?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unlike in Gabela, the conditions at Heliodrom from the 15th of December to the 15th of March, when I was there the conditions were significantly better.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you receive regular meals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had two meals a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you receive medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for medical care, we had some sort of male nurse. He was not really a doctor, but he was a male nurse. He could hand out pills when necessary. No doctor ever visited us until the 19th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How about sanitary facilities such as toilets and showers and water for washing? Were you provided with those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Heliodrom we had a normal toilet and we had normal conditions to take a shower, from the 15th of December. What happened before the 15th of December, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you permitted any visitors while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course not. You couldn't even think about it. Fighting was still going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And how long in total were you kept in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the 15th of December, 1993, to the 19th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And when you were released from Heliodrom did you walk out the gate or could you -- was the release done in a different format? Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our names were called out. We got out one by one. There were Red Cross vehicles parked outside, and they took us to the left side of the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: At the time of your release, could you give us a description of your condition? Were you suffering from any problems as a result of your incarceration from Kostana all the way through to Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I had health problems. I've already mentioned that I went to be examined by doctors, that I was found to suffer from consequences such as rib fractures, multiple rib fractures, damage to my brain centre for balance, and my right leg and right arm, my right hand, and the foot of my right leg go to sleep often.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How about your ribs? Did you sustain any injuries to your ribs during the period you were in custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The fifth, sixth, and the seventh rib on my right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And how did you sustain that injury in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I sustained those injuries from beatings in the Kostana hospital in Stolac. And this man, Marinko Maric, in Gabela finished me off.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You don't think you gave us any real detail about your involvement with Mr. Maric, Marinko. Could you briefly tell us what happened there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you didn't ask me. That's why I didn't say anything about it. I told you I was unconscious and paralysed. When I arrived in Gabela, at the very entrance to the camp I was taken to the interrogation room. In fact, I was carried in on a blanket that they just threw inside. This Marinko Maric knew my well, and one day, from what my relatives tell me, he tried to force me to get up. I was unable to get up, and he started kicking me. He didn't really care where he hit me. He kicked me like I was a football, including on the head. And some of the consequences that I am still suffering from must be from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you told us that you went to -- you went for medical aid afterwards. Can you tell us where you went and the name of the doctor who saw you after your release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the Velmos hospital and was seen by Dr. Hasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And as a -- did you -- did you have to have any operative treatment for your injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not have to have surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you have any sequelae? Did you have any injuries that you sustained during your time in these detention centres? Do they carry over to today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite a few consequences. I feel every change of weather in that my ribs, my ribcage hurts, and I have problems with my right arm and my right leg. And with age it's going to get worse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one technical question. Did you have an encephalography?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean my head?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: During your time in either Kostana, Gabela, or Heliodrom, do you remember if any of these camps or centres was ever visited by any VIP or senior government person from HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Nedjo Obradovic, Bozo Pavlovic, and Petar Matic visited us while we were together at Kostana hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But apart from these three that you mention, do you have a recollection of anybody else visiting you in Kostana or in Gabela or in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody, not once. If you mean high-ranking officials, nobody ever came to visit us in all the time we stayed there. From the moment I arrived and for the period that I was there, I can tell you for sure that nobody ever came to visit us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Apart from the complaints that you related to the panel about the injuries, did you have any markings on your body as a result of your detentions in any of the camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite a few. They extinguished cigarettes on my back, and I have burn marks on my back and elsewhere on my body where they did the same thing. That has been photographed, and the statement I made was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: That was by the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And would it be true to say that with the passage of time fortunately these burn marks, the blemishes have almost disappeared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's on my back and on my neck, so I can't see it very well, but it has swollen somehow. I can feel it with my hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I don't think I have any further questions for the witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Since the Defence has two hours, that makes 20 minutes per Defence counsel. We have 15 minutes left. Who wants to start? Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have given our time to Mr. Coric and Mr. Stojic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have given 10 minutes to Mr. Coric and 10 minutes to Mr. Stojic. So both of them have half an hour each. Who wants to continue? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours. Again, we have no questions. We wish to thank the gentleman. But we believe that Mr. Praljak wishes to use our time. We have no objections to that. We again urge Mr. Praljak to be as precise and focused as he should be and as he's been lately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to use up the 15 minutes that we have left and possibly continue tomorrow, or maybe if you think that's possible I might even conclude today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Go ahead now, because normally you have 30 minutes, 20 of yours plus 10 that you have been given, and maybe you are going to hand us the documents that you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to make sure that I'm going to have the time left today. Can I ask the usher?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you want -- if you can finish in 15 minutes, I can only applaud that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hardly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will just ask you a couple of questions while we are in open session, without mentioning any names. I'll start from the end of your testimony and then go back to the beginning of your evidence. In Heliodrom, where were you actually placed when you arrived, what kind of building? You told us several times that it applied from the 15th of December when you arrived. You don't know what it was like before the 15th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. I was in the building of the central prison, the central prison which housed members of the army on the first and second floor. On the third floor there were women, female inmates.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have to make a second's pause between questions and answers. Did you have mattresses? Did you have enough water in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did, both mattresses and water.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did any of the guards beat you while you were there in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was not beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In your statement given to the OTP, on page 11 in the Croatian version, which is page 7 in English, the bottom of page 7, you described it the following way: "Every day we were able to take a shower and use the toilet at our convenience. It felt almost like a good hotel."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way I described it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And that's how you experienced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Compared with the others, Gabela, Kostana, the hospital, that's how you can describe it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Let us now go back to the 3rd of July, 1993. You said that you were on leave at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who gave you that leave and how long was the leave? Did it begin on the 3rd or earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That leave started on the 3rd. I had my superior officer who granted me leave. I was duly replaced by someone else, and I left.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, how long was that leave supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seven, eight days, because there were lorries in reserve, on standby, and I was on standby, and I could be engaged when the need arose. I was supposed to come to the assembly point, a specific place where I was supposed to report in case I was called.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You told us that Arif Zele was one of the 16 people with whom you were arrested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Wait a minute. I didn't finish my question. You said he was also a member of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was he also on official leave? Do you know anything about that? Were you in the same unit together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were together in the same brigade but not the same unit. I think he was a soldier on the front line, and I was a driver.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You don't know how he happened to find himself in that group of 16 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I don't have enough time, and the Judges asked you a lot of questions about it. I, too, am confused, though, by your movements given with the 3rd, and I'll try to ask the most important things. You said that you were at Rotimlja and that you did what you were ordered to do from the 3rd to the 6th. That was said on page 25, lines 10 and 11. What were you doing and who ordered you to do these things? So who is issuing the records, because I understand you were on leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had my superior, and whatever needed to be done at Rotimlja I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That was the period from the 3rd to the 6th when you were on leave. Was it then that you were doing those errands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was talking about the 3rd, because I said I departed on the 3rd in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You mentioned the 3rd of July. You have to remember how it was. So when was it that you were at Rotimlja, because you just said a moment -- just let me finish, please. You said, "On the 3rd I was granted leave. My leave began. It was supposed to be seven days long." Then you said, "Within three days I went to Rotimlja and did as I was ordered to do." So since you were on leave, who was it who let you know that there were things you needed to do? Who was that superior, and what did you actually do at Rotimlja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the errands that needed to be done, and take this to a bunker, take another shipment somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Am I concluding correctly that your superior called you up, although you were on leave, let you know that there were some errands that needed to be done and that's what you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I got a message.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The message that you should come and do these errands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You say in your statement that you decided to go into hiding in the woods.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us whose decision it was? When you say "we," do you mean your family or the larger group of 16, 17 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The larger group. It was a majority decision among us. And we were all thinking and hoping that it was going to end soon. We had a power generator with us. We had a radio and cassette player. We listened to the news, and we heard on the news that it was going to be all over soon, that everybody would be able to go back to their homes, and that's why we stayed in hiding, hoping that -- and expecting that it would be over soon. And that goes for everybody, my mother and the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that you stayed under tents. So you had brought tents with you. Military tents you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was simple nylon, plastic. We made makeshift tents out of them. Those were not proper tents. It was just plastic that we made stand up on sticks.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I see. When you say, "we decided," how did that come about that you gathered, the 16 of you? Did you have a meeting? Did you have some sort of communication amongst you? Did -- were you all from the same village? How did you come to that decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all from the same village, and there was no nobody on the outside advising us or telling us what to do. We decided that on our own.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who was your commander in Bregava Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Bajro Pizovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said yourself that you were not involved in the fighting with the Serbs, you personally were not involved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What about the Bregava Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you knew, what was the larger zone of responsibility of the Bregava Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you tell it us what area that covered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area overlooking Rotimlja village. From that point until Semica Gredina, up to the positions of the HVO. That's what we held. I don't know how large it was, but it wasn't very large.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that you joined the Bregava Brigade in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that from August 1992 when you became a soldier and a member of that brigade, until July, the relations between you and the HVO were quite good? There were no conflicts and no military clashes? I don't know about interpersonal relations, but your brigade had no conflicts with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did not, not that I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The same probably applies to January 1993. Would that be fair to conclude? You say from August 1992 until July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know, not now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In that period from July 1993 -- sorry, from August 1992 until July 1993, did you take part in any clashes with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you hear about anyone else in your unit or in your brigade who did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
